name: Aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy
lead: For appearance, ALA PDT is used in dermatology clinics to treat sun-damaged skin and pre-cancerous spots on the face and scalp, and it has been studied for acne and rosacea. Reviews of the technique note that, besides being effective, it is associated with excellent cosmetic outcomes, which is why it appeals as an alternative to destructive treatments on visible skin [9].

Aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy (ALA PDT) is a procedure in which aminolevulinic acid, a precursor of heme, is applied to the skin and the area is then illuminated with a specific light source. The skin converts ALA into protoporphyrin IX, a light-sensitive compound that produces reactive oxygen species when illuminated and damages targeted cells.[1][2]

In the United States the topical ALA product Ameluz, used with a red-light lamp, is labelled for actinic keratoses on the face and scalp and for superficial basal cell carcinoma; acne is not a labelled indication.[2] Use for acne is described as still under clinical investigation, with a 2016 systematic review calling it a safe and effective method and one phase II trial finding it not superior to blue/violet light alone.[1]
Common side effects are application-site redness, pain and burning, and a period of photosensitivity.[1][2]

paras: ALA is a non-proteinogenic amino acid made in the body as the first committed precursor in heme synthesis.[3] When supplied from outside, it is converted to protoporphyrin IX (PpIX), which accumulates in the skin; red or blue light of suitable wavelength then activates it.[2][3]

Related esters such as methyl aminolevulinate (Metvix) exist, and ALA clears from the skin in about 24 hours, which is described as limiting prolonged photosensitivity compared with older photosensitizers.[1]

Labelled dermatologic uses of Ameluz PDT are lesion- and field-directed treatment of mild-to-moderate actinic keratoses and treatment of superficial basal cell carcinoma in adults.[2] Oral ALA is also used for fluorescence-guided resection of glioma.[4]

Dermatology literature has studied ALA PDT for acne, photodamage and related concerns. According to Wikipedia's summary, results suggest benefit mainly in severe acne, and treatment may cause severe redness and moderate-to-severe pain or burning.[1]

Treatment involves applying the photosensitizer, allowing time for it to be converted to protoporphyrin IX, and then illuminating the area with a suitable light source, in a clinic setting [2][9]. The 2006 dermatology review noted that efficacy is limited mainly by how deeply the photosensitizer and the activating light penetrate, while describing ALA PDT as safe, well tolerated and effective for many dermatologic conditions, with the strongest data for actinic damage [10].

A 2022 review in Biochemical Society Transactions describes how burning, stinging and prickling during illumination have restricted use, and presents daylight PDT, in which sunlight is the light source, as a protocol that has produced some of the best results for treatment response and patient satisfaction in multiple or confluent actinic keratoses [9]. A 2023 randomized trial in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology compared ALA PDT with no incubation against one-hour incubation for actinic keratosis [12].

Beyond actinic keratosis and acne, ALA PDT has been studied in rosacea, where a 2023 single-center randomized, evaluator-blind study compared it with minocycline in moderate-to-severe disease [13]. It has also been examined in psoriasis, genital vitiligo, plantar warts and an acneform rash induced by erlotinib, as well as oral lichen planus [14][15][16][17][18][19]. A systematic review of PDT for skin carcinomas pooled 17 randomized trials with 2,166 participants and mostly used methyl aminolevulinate or ALA as photosensitizers, noting few studies per comparison [20]. The Cochrane review of light therapies for acne set out to explore the effects of light of different wavelengths on acne, searching for randomized trials through 2015 [21].

The Ameluz label lists application-site erythema, pain/burning and irritation as the most common reactions, and warns of hypersensitivity, transient amnestic episodes, lamp-related eye injury and increased photosensitivity; patients and providers must wear eye protection.[2] The label reports no identified pregnancy-related risk from the limited data available, with low systemic absorption.[2]

Registered dermatology trials of ALA PDT found in the registry concern actinic keratosis and photodamage rather than acne: a phase 2 trial of topical ALA PDT for actinic keratosis (n=105)[5], a phase 4 daylight-PDT comparison of BF-200 ALA with a methyl ester (n=72)[6], and a small phase 1 study of Ameluz activated with a broadband light for actinic keratoses and photodamage (n=10).[7]

For acne, a 2016 systematic review described PDT as safe and effective, whereas a phase II trial found it not superior to blue/violet light alone.[1] The oncology literature on ALA PDT is larger.[4][8]

card.summary: A clinic procedure pairing topical ALA with light to treat actinic keratoses; its acne use is investigational, with mixed trial signals.
card.note: Clinic-only; pain, redness and photosensitivity are common; acne is not a labelled use.

quick.overview:
ALA PDT applies a heme precursor to the skin, then shines light on it so the skin's own conversion product destroys targeted cells. Its labelled dermatology uses are actinic keratosis and superficial basal cell carcinoma.

For acne it is still described as investigational: a 2016 systematic review was favourable, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue/violet light alone.
quick.mechanism: ALA becomes protoporphyrin IX in skin cells; light activates it in the presence of oxygen, producing reactive oxygen species that damage cells.
quick.risks: Common effects are redness, pain or burning and photosensitivity. The label also warns of hypersensitivity, transient amnestic episodes and eye injury from the lamp; eye protection is required.

chain: Clinic applies ALA to the skin
Skin cells convert it to a light-sensitive compound
Red or blue light activates it and damages targeted cells
Clearer, less sun-damaged or less inflamed skin
angle.text: A clinician applies ALA, waits for it to be converted in the skin, then illuminates the area. Labelled uses are sun-damage lesions on the face and scalp; acne and rosacea use is under study.
